title: Names carry people
hook: Ashkenazim often name after relatives who have died, Sephardim often after living grandparents

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was brit milah, and your line was the covenant. At the end of that morning, a name was spoken aloud for the first time. Where does a name like that come from? Day one thousand two hundred ninety-four.

Two families, two baby boys, the same week. In the first family, the baby is named after his great-grandfather, who died last spring. When the name is announced, his grandmother starts to cry, and then to laugh. In the second family, the baby is named after his grandfather, who is standing right there in the front row, holding the camera and suddenly unable to work it. Two families, two customs, two very different moments. And underneath both of them, the same conviction. Today's line is that conviction.
screen: `A NAME FROM THE ONE WHO DIED.` → `A NAME FROM THE ONE IN THE FRONT ROW.` → `THE SAME CONVICTION.`

segments.voice: Names carry people. Turn it four ways. First, the Ashkenazi custom. Jews whose families come from Central and Eastern Europe have often named children after relatives who have died, and often avoided naming after anyone still living. The name becomes a way to keep someone present. A grandmother who never met the baby is named aloud every time the child is called to dinner. Second, the Sephardi custom. Jews whose families come from Spain, North Africa and the Middle East have often done the opposite: they name children after living grandparents. To hear your own name given to a grandchild, while you are alive to hear it, is a great honor. One custom carries the dead forward. The other crowns the living. Both say the same thing: a child doesn't arrive from nowhere. Third, the old roots. In Genesis, when Jacob blesses his grandsons, he asks that his own name, and the names of Abraham and Isaac, be named in them. Long before either custom, a grandfather wanted to live on in the children's names. And Proverbs puts it plainly, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "A good name is rather to be chosen than great riches." Fourth, the name you earn. A midrash teaches that every person has three names: the one their parents give, the one other people call them, and the one they acquire for themselves, and the last is the best. The family can hand down a name. Only a life can fill it.
screen: `NAMED FOR THE ONES WHO DIED.` · `NAMED FOR THE ONES STILL HERE.` · `LET MY NAME BE NAMED IN THEM.` · `THE NAME YOU ACQUIRE.` · then, large: `NAMES CARRY PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn your name's story. Settle, and breathe. Say your own first name quietly, once. Ask what you know about it. Who chose it? Were you named for someone? Was there a name they almost gave you instead? If you know, let that person come to mind and sit with them a moment. If you don't know, notice the question, and who you could ask. Then think of the third name, the one you're earning. What would you want it to say? The bell holds the time.
Names carry people. Named for the dead, or for the living, and then filled by a life. Today's word.
Your line: names carry people. Today, ask someone who would know how you got your name, and listen to the whole story. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-four.

notes: Proverbs 22:1 quoted from JPS 1917; confirm exact wording.
Genesis 48:16 paraphrased ('let my name be named in them, and the name of my fathers Abraham and Isaac').
Ashkenazi and Sephardi naming customs stated with 'often', as the index does; the 'set order' of Sephardi naming (e.g. first son after paternal grandfather) is kept general. Confirm.
The three-names midrash paraphrased; confirm citation (Kohelet Rabbah 7:1 / Tanchuma Vayakhel 1) and that 'the last is the best' is fair.
Hook families are illustrative, not a real event.
